record.paper_title: Heterogeneous Computing: Goals, Methods, and Open Problems
record.original_question: For heterogeneous computing suites, what hierarchical scheduling techniques can make it possible to scale the suite up to very large sizes?

evidence.quote: Distributed high-performance heterogeneous computing (HC) environments are composed of machines with varied computational capabilities interconnected by high-speed links.
Hierarchical scheduling techniques are under development to allow for HC suites to be scaled up to very large sizes.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a heterogeneous computing (HC) suite, defined as a distributed collection of machines with varied computational capabilities interconnected by high-speed communication links, on which a stream of tasks (each with possibly different execution-time profiles on different machines, and with arbitrary inter-task data dependencies and quality-of-service requirements) must be matched to machines and scheduled in time. A scheduling policy must decide, for each arriving task or task graph, which machine should execute each task and in what order, with the objective of optimizing system-wide performance metrics such as makespan, throughput, robustness, or weighted quality of service.

Design and analyze hierarchical scheduling techniques — that is, scheduling architectures organized into multiple coordinated levels (for example, a global/top-level scheduler that partitions or delegates work among regional sub-schedulers, which in turn dispatch to local machine-level schedulers) — that allow such an HC suite to be scaled up to very large sizes (in the number of machines, in the rate of incoming tasks, and in geographic/network extent) while maintaining acceptable scheduling quality and bounded scheduling overhead.

Specifically: (i) Specify a hierarchical scheduling framework (levels, information flow between levels, decision granularity, and aggregation of machine-state and task-state information) suitable for very large heterogeneous suites. (ii) Prove or empirically demonstrate scalability properties, such as sublinear growth of scheduling overhead and information-exchange cost as the number of machines grows. (iii) Quantify the loss in solution quality (relative to a hypothetical centralized optimal scheduler) introduced by the hierarchy, and identify regimes in which this loss is provably small.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction in heterogeneous/distributed computing rather than a precisely formulated mathematical conjecture. Hierarchical scheduling for large-scale heterogeneous systems remains an active research area (with ongoing work in grid, cloud, edge, and HPC scheduling), and no single definitive solution has been established. Hence the problem is best classified as open.
